guide.summary: Custom OAuth app, unpublished, customer orgs (self-serve (no review step found in the docs)); Published in Box Integrations (app review).
guide.verdict: Easiest: Custom OAuth app, unpublished, customer orgs (self-serve (no review step found in the docs)). Hardest: Published in Box Integrations (app review).

composio.note: Composio offers a managed OAuth app for Box, fine for prototypes. For launch, create an auth config with your own client ID and secret, and copy the redirect URI from the Composio dashboard.

need_own_app.answer: Not for prototypes, since Composio manages a Box OAuth app. For launch, use your own app if you want your branding, your own scopes, a dedicated quota or shorter polling intervals.
reasons: Consent screen shows your brand instead of Composio's
Dedicated rate-limit quota instead of shared quota
Polling shorter than the 15-minute managed minimum

prerequisites.title: Box developer account
prerequisites.detail: A free developer account gives access to the Developer Console. MFA must be on for the account to view the client secret.

prerequisites.title: Pick the User app type
prerequisites.detail: User apps use OAuth 2.0 and cannot be converted to Server apps later.

steps.title: Create a User app
steps.detail: In the Developer Console choose New App, then User type, then Create.

steps.title: Choose minimal scopes
steps.detail: Draft the minimal scope list the agent needs. Scopes are set in the Developer Console.
steps.done_when: Scopes are saved on the app

steps.title: Copy Composio redirect URI
steps.detail: Copy the redirect URI from the Composio dashboard and add it in the OAuth 2.0 Redirect URI section. It must match exactly.

steps.title: Create Composio auth config
steps.detail: Create the auth config through Composio's API with your client ID and secret.

steps.title: Ask customer admins to enable app
steps.detail: Give the customer's Box Admin your Client ID if their settings require enablement.
steps.done_when: The app shows as enabled in their Admin Console

steps.title: Submit for Box Integrations review
steps.detail: Submit the production-ready app in the Developer Console and complete the checklist.

traps.title: Each new Box enterprise can authorize up to 10,000
traps.detail: Each new Box enterprise can authorize up to 10,000 custom apps.

traps.title: A developer token generated in the console has a
traps.detail: A developer token generated in the console has a 60-minute lifetime and is meant for development only.

traps.title: Refresh tokens are valid for 60 days or one
traps.detail: Refresh tokens are valid for 60 days or one use (general rule on this page, not specific to testing mode).

traps.title: Customer admins may block the app
traps.detail: If an enterprise turns on Disable unpublished apps by default, an admin must explicitly enable your OAuth app.

traps.title: Scope changes need re-authorization
traps.detail: Changed scopes do not take effect until the app is re-authorized. Enterprise developers must submit for admin re-authorization.

traps.title: Redirect URI must match exactly
traps.detail: A missing redirect_uri with multiple URIs configured gives a redirect_uri_missing error.

traps.title: API calls count toward customer allotment
traps.detail: Calls from custom apps count toward the enterprise's monthly API allocation; partner integrations do not.

blockers.what_it_means: The enterprise may disable unpublished apps by default.
blockers.what_to_do: Send the customer's Box Admin your Client ID to enable it.

evidence.question: G4
evidence.quote: Downscoping, also known as Token Exchange, is our mechanism by which developers can restrict the permissions on the Access Token to a more granular level, allowing them to build out their own permissions model on Box Platform.
evidence.answer: For Box UI Elements, downscoping (Token Exchange) lets developers restrict the Access Token's permissions to a more granular level.

evidence.question: G4
evidence.quote: So a developer can combine multiple scopes in a token exchange request to generate a token with the desired set of functionality.
evidence.answer: Box's UI Element scopes are designed to be modular and strictly additive, so multiple scopes can be combined in one token exchange request.

evidence.question: G4
evidence.quote: This scope should always be included in the Token Exchange request.
evidence.answer: Each Box UI Element has a base scope that gives the least set of permissions needed for that element to work, and it must always be included in the token exchange request.

evidence.question: G4
evidence.quote: Since the base set of permissions for every UI Element to functionally work may not be the same (Content Uploader UI Element doesn't require preview permissions, for example), UI Elements may have their own respective base scopes.
evidence.answer: Base scopes can differ between UI Elements; for example, the Content Uploader UI Element does not require preview permissions.

evidence.question: G4
evidence.quote: As with base scopes, feature scopes too are mostly different for every UI Element.
evidence.answer: Beyond the base scope, Box UI Elements have feature scopes that add capabilities when paired with the base scope; feature scopes are mostly different for each UI Element.

evidence.question: G4
evidence.quote: So even if some end-user of your application uses the token directly against the API, they can't gain access beyond what you intended them to provide through the UI Element.
evidence.answer: Box UI Element scopes are meant to contain only the minimum permissions needed for their action, so a token holder using the API directly cannot gain access beyond what the UI Element grants.

evidence.question: G4
evidence.quote: So adding this scope to the token enables the specific action.
evidence.answer: Each Box UI Element scope maps directly to a specific action in the UI Element, so adding the scope to a token enables that action.
